entries.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
entries.purpose: tomb of Pharaoh Khufu
layout: square base 230 m on a side, aligned to the cardinal directions
corbelled internal galleries and chambers
original polished limestone casing was stripped for later Cairo buildings
entries.found: on the Giza plateau west of Cairo; the last surviving Seven Wonder
entries.notes: Was 146.6 m tall when cased; now about 139 m. A wonder for 3,800 years, it is the yardstick for every big masonry ruin.

entries.name: Stonehenge
entries.purpose: ritual and burial monument; solstice alignment
layout: concentric rings: bank and ditch, sarsen circle with lintels, inner horseshoe of trilithons, bluestone rings
avenue leads from the river Avon to the north-east; heel stone on the solstice axis
blueprint: legend: h upright stone (4 m), . grass; schematic only - real circle is 33 m across with lintels
entries.found: on the Salisbury Plain chalk grassland, Wiltshire
entries.notes: Built and rebuilt in phases over ~1,500 years; sarsens average 20 t, the biggest ~30-45 t. Pair it with an earthen bank and ditch, never with a roof.

entries.name: Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre)
entries.purpose: amphitheatre for gladiatorial games and spectacles
layout: oval ring, 189 m by 156 m, four storeys, the top two with pilasters rather than arches
tiered seating around a sand-covered arena over a two-level service maze
entries.found: in central Rome, on the former lake of Nero's Golden House
entries.notes: Held 50,000-80,000 spectators. The hypogeum (tunnels, cages, lifts) is often more ruin-like than the famous facade; earthquakes dropped the south wall.

entries.name: Parthenon (Athenian Acropolis)
entries.purpose: temple of Athena Parthenos; treasury of the Delian League
parts: cella with colossal Athena chryselephantine statue
layout: rectangular peripteral temple, 8 by 17 columns, on a 3-step platform
columns lean inward and the stylobate curves to correct optical illusion
entries.found: atop the Athenian Acropolis limestone plateau
entries.notes: Never fully ruined on purpose: mosque 1456, ammunition store under the Ottomans, blown up by Venetian shell in 1687. Close enough to Athens that tourists fill it by 10 am.

entries.name: Pompeii
entries.purpose: Roman port town; buried by Vesuvius
layout: rough oval walled city at the foot of Mount Vesuvius
graffiti, shopfronts and intact upper storeys survive because it was sealed in 4-6 m of ash and pumice
entries.found: in Campania, 23 km south-east of Naples; one of Italy's most visited ruins
entries.notes: The most complete frozen Roman town; plaster casts of victims are the signature object. Best archaeological argument for 'leave it as found'.

entries.name: Machu Picchu
entries.purpose: royal estate of Emperor Pachacuti; ceremonial centre
layout: split into agricultural lower terraces and urban upper sector by the central plaza
fine ashlar masonry without mortar, fitted so closely a blade cannot enter
entries.found: on a saddle between Huayna Picchu and Machu Picchu mountain at 2,430 m; reached by train or a multi-day Inca Trail
entries.notes: Abandoned ~100 years after construction, never looted by the Spanish. Fragile stonework: visitors erode paths, so cap daily numbers.

entries.name: Angkor Wat
entries.purpose: state temple-mountain for Khmer Suryavarman II; later Buddhist monastery
layout: temple-mountain in three tiers inside a 1,500 m-by-1,300 m moat
Central tower 65 m above the plain; bas-reliefs of the Churning of the Sea of Milk
entries.found: north of Siem Reap, Cambodia; largest religious monument ever built
entries.notes: Originally Hindu; gradually Theravada Buddhist from ~13th century. Trees threading through walls are the signature look; root pressure is what is pulling it down.

entries.name: Petra (Al-Khazneh, Siq and the Monastery)
entries.purpose: Nabataean capital and caravan trade hub; rock-cut facades and tombs
layout: a desert wadi system walled and terraced into a city; facades carved top-down into rose sandstone cliffs
water channels and cisterns everywhere - Petra survived by engineering scarce rain
entries.found: in southern Jordan; 'Rose-red city' reached through a narrow gorge after a 2 km walk
entries.notes: Al-Khazneh is the most photographed ruin in the Middle East. Footprint covers the famed core only; the Nabataean city stretched for miles through the hills.

entries.name: Roman Forum
entries.purpose: civic, political and religious centre of Rome
layout: valley floor between the Palatine and Capitoline hills, packed layer over layer for 1,000 years
collapsing columns, spolia and stratified pavements - a stack of eras more than a single building
entries.found: in central Rome between the Colosseum and Capitoline Hill; densest layered ruin on Earth
entries.notes: The ultimate 'layered city' ruin: Republican pavements, Imperial arches, medieval churches inside temples, Renaissance digs. Expect rubble mixed with standing colonnades.

entries.name: Tikal
entries.purpose: major Maya city-state; ceremonial funerary pyramids and royal court
parts: Temple I (Temple of the Great Jaguar)
layout: twin-pyramid complexes grouped around civic plazas; stelae and altars in front of temples
Temple I rises 47 m with nine tiers and a roof comb carved with the ruler's face
entries.found: in the Petén rainforest of northern Guatemala; howler monkeys and toucans nest on the ruins
entries.notes: Among the largest Maya cities; roof combs make the silhouette. Site is UNESCO-listed with jungle growing back over plazas - dense, green, and wet.

entries.name: Chichen Itza (El Castillo)
entries.purpose: Maya political and ceremonial capital; equinox serpent of shadows
layout: flat open plaza with the stepped pyramid at one end; nine terraces with 91 steps per side plus the top platform = 365
at the equinoxes a shadow serpent descends the northern staircase
entries.found: in the Yucatán lowlands, Mexico; one of the New Seven Wonders
entries.notes: The serpent-shadow equinox event is the marquee moment. Open, flat, exposed ruins in bright limestone - the opposite of Tikal's jungle shade.

entries.name: Teotihuacan
entries.purpose: mesoamerican sacred metropolis; Pyramids of the Sun and Moon
layout: gridded city along the 4 km Avenue of the Dead, oriented to the mountains
pyramids echo the volcanic skyline; apartment compounds spread in a 20 km2 grid
entries.found: 45 km north-east of Mexico City; once held 125,000+ people - among the largest cities on Earth c. 450 CE
entries.notes: Nobody knows the builders' name. Buried later under Aztec veneration. Talud-tablero tiered wall profiles are the diagnostic style.

entries.name: Easter Island moai and ahu
entries.purpose: ancestral statue platforms honouring chiefs and lineages
layout: rows of moai standing on stone ahu platforms, all facing inland toward settlements
nearly 900 moai cataloged; tallest erected ~10 m, heaviest ~80 t, most only 4-6 m
blueprint: layer 0: . . . . . . . . .|a a a a a a a a a
layer 1: . M . . M . . M .|a a a a a a a a a
legend: a ahu platform stone, M moai torso (tuff); schematic only, not to scale - real ahu carry 1 to 15 moai facing the land
entries.found: Rapa Nui (Chile), the most remote inhabited island on Earth; almost every statue faces away from the sea
entries.notes: Biome slotted as savanna grassland, but the island is windswept and near treeless - plan empty vistas, not forests. Many moai were toppled in the 18th-19th centuries; standing rows are the exception.

entries.name: Knossos (Palace of Minos)
entries.purpose: Minoan palace-complex and administrative centre; source of the labyrinth myth
layout: sprawling multi-storey palace around a rectangular central court, built in phases then destroyed c. 1450 BCE
Evans' 1900-1930 concrete 'restoration' now reads as the ruin itself
entries.found: on low hills south of Heraklion, Crete; reached by city bus from the port
entries.notes: Part functional excavation, part 20th-century fancy - original height unknown, so height_m is null. Timber-framed, earthquake-resistant masonry; many walls were painted vivid red and blue.

entries.name: Mycenae (Lion Gate and Citadel)
entries.purpose: Mycenaean fortress-palace of Agamemnon; heroic bronze-age capital
layout: fortified hilltop citadel above the Argive plain; wall blocks up to 12 t, fitted without mortar
gate lintel ~20 t, relief triangle above with two confronted lions
entries.found: north-east of Argos, Peloponnese; surmounted by the palace ruins
entries.notes: The Lion Gate is the signature piece to model. Cyclopean blocks explain the legend that Cyclops built it; Treasury of Atreus nearby is a corbelled tholos tomb, c. 1250 BCE.

entries.name: Göbekli Tepe
entries.purpose: hunter-gatherer ritual enclosures; oldest monumental architecture known
layout: circular and oval enclosures 10-30 m across set into a 15 m-high artificial tell
two central pillars up to 5.5 m, each ~8-10 t, ringed by smaller inward-facing pillars
entries.found: on a limestone plateau in south-east Turkey; 15 km north-east of Şanlıurfa
entries.notes: Built before farming, pottery or villages - it rewrote prehistory. Enclosures were deliberately backfilled; much of the site remains buried. Steep slope to model: it is a hill, not a hole.

entries.name: Çatalhöyük
entries.purpose: one of the first permanent dense proto-urban settlements on Earth
layout: houses packed wall-to-wall with no streets; people entered through roof holes
dead buried beneath house floors; walls replastered and painted generation after generation
entries.found: in the Konya plain of central Turkey; a low 15 m mound rising from flat farmland
entries.notes: No streets at all - model solid wall-to-wall buildings with flat roofs, ladders and hearth smoke. Population estimated 5,000-8,000 at its peak.

entries.name: Mohenjo-daro
entries.purpose: Indus capital city; grid-planned with drains, wells and a great bath
layout: orthogonal grid of baked-brick streets on a raised flood platform; 250 ha built-up area
Citadel walls above; lower town in a strict grid; standardized brick ratio 1:2:4 throughout
entries.found: on the Indus floodplain in Sindh, Pakistan; about 500 km north of Karachi
entries.notes: Population ~40,000 - one of the largest cities on Earth c. 2000 BCE. Brick ruins stand like canyon walls after stripping wind-blown soil; salt weathering is the active killer.

entries.name: Persepolis
entries.purpose: Achaemenid ceremonial capital; New Year audience hall
layout: half-built on an 18 m-high terraced platform at the foot of Kuh-e Rahmat, the rest free-standing
processional stairs with low-relief crowds of subject peoples bringing gifts
entries.found: in the Marvdasht plain of Fars, Iran; burned by Alexander the Great in 330 BCE
entries.notes: The platform, towering columns and columned halls are the silhouette - not a buried city but a grand ruined podium. Oxen-led pillar stones are visible everywhere.

entries.name: Babylon (Ishtar Gate and Processional Way)
entries.purpose: capital of the Neo-Babylonian Empire; Nebuchadnezzar's parade city
layout: walled city straddling the Euphrates; walls 12-24 m high and 17-22 m thick in Nebuchadnezzar's time, 950 ha inside them
Ishtar Gate 15 m high, glazed blue with lions, bulls and mushussu dragons
entries.found: 90 km south of Baghdad on the Euphrates; Babil tell still visible as low mounds
entries.notes: The Ishtar Gate in Berlin's Pergamonmuseum is the real thing; on site today is a partial reconstruction. Ziggurat Etemenanki was ~90 m tall and was recycled into Baghdad.

entries.name: Palmyra (Tadmor)
entries.purpose: oasis caravan city; Rome's frontier pivot; short-lived desert empire under Queen Zenobia
layout: planned oasis caravan halt with a colonnaded main street running through the centre
tower tombs line the approach roads like a necropolis skyline
entries.found: in the Syrian steppe; the colonnade vanished under bushes by the 1700s until 20th-century digging
entries.notes: Deliberately destroyed in 2015 and partly rebuilt - a ruin of a ruin. Colonnade, arch and tower tombs are the silhouette pieces to reuse.

entries.name: Baalbek (Temple of Bacchus and Temple of Jupiter)
entries.purpose: Roman imperial sanctuary; Jupiter, Bacchus and Venus temples
layout: monumental precinct with a forecourt and three temples on a raised terrace in the Beqaa valley
Temple of Jupiter: 54 columns 19 m tall on a 88 by 46 m podium; the trilithon slabs each weigh ~800 t
entries.found: in the Beqaa valley, Lebanon; the giant trilithon stones are the most photographed 'impossible' blocks in antiquity
entries.notes: Bacchus is the best-preserved Roman temple anywhere - its roof beams fell leaving the interior perfect shade. Column mega-blocks make this a masonry-and-ramp fantasy build.

entries.name: Ephesus (Celsus Library and Great Theatre)
entries.purpose: Greek-Roman port city; cult of Artemis; provincial capital
parts: Temple of Artemis (nearby, one column left)
layout: wide marble street between theater and library, lined with porticoes, fountains and statues
Celsus facade two storeys with four aediculaed doorways; niches once held 3 large statues of Celsus
entries.found: on the Aegean coast of Turkey, 3 km from Selçuk; once a harbour, now silt has moved the shoreline 10 km west
entries.notes: One column of the Temple of Artemis - a Seven Wonder - stands a few km away. Celsus' two-storey trabeated facade is the single most photogenic library facade in the ancient world.

entries.name: Carnac alignments and menhirs
entries.purpose: megalithic alignments; probably astronomical and funerary
layout: parallel rows running west-east, stones tapering from 4 m at one end to under 1 m at the other, terminating in a semicircular cromlech
Ménec row: 11 rows over ~1.1 km; the whole Carnac landscape once held thousands of stones
blueprint: layer 0: . . . . . . . . . . . . . .|m . m . m . m . m . m .|m . . m . . m . . m . .|m m m m m m m m m m m m m
legend: m granite menhir (0.5-6 m), . heath; schematic only - real rows run in parallel for over a kilometre
entries.found: on the Brittany coast around Carnac, France; stones never moved more than a few km from source granite beds
entries.notes: Whether an astronomical calendar or a show of territorial power is still argued. Field is legally protected and fenced off; expect vandalism history. Great for 'mysterious dolmens in a field' moments.

entries.name: Newgrange
entries.purpose: chambered passage tomb; winter solstice sunrise alignment
layout: kidney-shaped cairn facing a river bend; entrance corridor with a roof-box aimed at the winter solstice sunrise
97 kerbstones ring the base; many incised with spirals and megalithic art
blueprint: legend: q kerb/cairn edge, d doorway with roof-box, . grass; the solstice ray enters the doorway and strikes the back recess
entries.found: in the Boyne valley, County Meath, Ireland; older than both Stonehenge and the pyramids
entries.notes: Inside at dawn on ~Dec 19-23, light travels 19 m to the central chamber - one of the oldest astronomical alignments on Earth. Bring a torch; the passage is tight.

entries.name: Mesa Verde (Cliff Palace)
entries.purpose: cliff aerie housing; defensive and ceremonial
layout: about 150 rooms stacked into a south-facing cliff alcove in five to six storeys
kivas and rooms share roof terraces; access only by ladder from above
entries.found: Mesa Verde National Park, Colorado, USA; 600+ cliff dwellings in the park
entries.notes: Abandoned in the 13th-century drought; inhabitants walked away and never came back. Adobe and timber floors are mostly gone - expect exposed ledges and circular kiva walls.

entries.name: Chaco Canyon (Pueblo Bonito)
entries.purpose: great house; trade, ritual and administration hub of the Chaco world
layout: semicircular D-plan, back to the north canyon wall; nearly 800 rooms over 4 storeys, 32+ kivas
aligns to solstices and lunar cycles; an engineering-and-masonry shock for its era
entries.found: NW New Mexico, USA; a barren high desert canyon reachable only by unpaved roads
entries.notes: Chacoans hauled ~200,000 pine logs 80 km from the Chuska mountains. The D shape is the giveaway; great houses were empty-ish ceremonial hubs, not full towns.

entries.name: Cahokia (Monks Mound and the Grand Plaza)
entries.purpose: Mississippian chiefdom capital; platform mounds for civic-ceremonial buildings
layout: planned grid of mounds and plazas around Monks Mound on the Mississippi floodplain
Monks Mound base nearly as big as the Great Pyramid; a wooden chief's house stood on the summit
blueprint: legend: # post hole of a Woodhenge circle (theoretical), . grass field; schematic - Monks Mound itself is 316 m long and 30 m high of packed earth
entries.found: near Collinsville, Illinois, across the Mississippi from St Louis; most mounds now grassed over
entries.notes: Population 10,000-20,000 at its peak - bigger than London c. 1100 CE. Most mounds look like grassy hills today; the grandeur is invisible without interpretation.

entries.name: Great Zimbabwe (Great Enclosure)
entries.purpose: Shona royal capital; trade hub linking goldfields to the Swahili coast
layout: an oval great enclosure of curved dry-stone walls with no straight lines, no mortar, no foundations
granite courses 1-2 m thick; the Conical Tower rises like a granary but its purpose is ritual
entries.found: 1450 km north of Cape Town, Zimbabwe; the largest stone ruins south of the Sahara besides West Africa
entries.notes: Colonnaded curved walls that lean inwards slightly; no mortar anywhere. Europeans wrongly claimed outsiders built it - the site proves the Shona built an empire.

entries.name: Hampi (Vijayanagara)
entries.purpose: Vijayanagara imperial capital; temples, bazaars and palaces
layout: a sprawling sacred city of granite boulders: temple tank, pillared halls and walled palace courts strung between hills
Vittala chariot is the iconic photo; hundreds of fallen columns lie in rows like a petrified army
entries.found: in Karnataka, south India; a 25 km2 scatter of temples among giant boulder hills
entries.notes: Destroyed after the 1565 Battle of Talikota; looted and left ruined. Boulder-strewn terrain + temple towers make the 'place of ruins' landscape itself.

entries.name: Lalibela (Bete Giyorgis rock churches)
entries.purpose: New Jerusalem; eleven monolithic rock-hewn churches; living pilgrimage centre
layout: two clusters of churches cut DOWNWARD into the red tuff plateau, linked by trenches and tunnels
Bete Giyorgis: cross-shaped, 12 m across, freestanding inside a 25 by 25 m pit, carved from one block
blueprint: legend: t tuff wall, # hollow interior (pit), . open pit rim; schematic top-down view of Bete Giyorgis; the cross shape only reads from the air
entries.found: at 2,600 m on the Lasta plateau, Ethiopia; still a working Ethiopian Orthodox pilgrimage site
entries.notes: Eleven churches, most still used for services - this is a living ruin, not an abandoned one. Arrive at dawn; priests in white, pilgrims, and incense inside black rock.

entries.name: Axum stelae and obelisks
entries.purpose: royal funerary stelae and markers of tombs in the Aksumite capital
layout: a dense field of carved stelae over vaulted tombs; largest single piece was ~33 m and fell before it could be raised
obelisk was seized by Italy in 1937, returned to Axum in 2005 and re-erected
entries.found: in the northern Ethiopian highlands, 2,100 m up, near the town of Axum; bus from Adwa or Gondar
entries.notes: Carved false doors and windows - they imitate storeyed Aksumite palaces in granite. Aksumite stelae are the African answer to Egyptian obelisks.

entries.name: Sigiriya (Lion Rock)
entries.purpose: rock fortress palace of King Kassapa I
layout: a 200 m-high free-standing inselberg with galleries cut into its faces and a palace on top
lion paws flank the stairway landing; frescoes survive in a sheltered hollow mid-way up
entries.found: in the dry zone of Sri Lanka, ~150 km north-east of Colombo; climb is 1,200 steps
entries.notes: The fortress was actually a refuge palace - the approach courts, gardens and moat are half the experience. Mirror Wall was polished so well you could see your face in it.

entries.name: Ayutthaya
entries.purpose: Siamese capital for 400 years; temples, palaces, river trade
layout: ruined temples and prangs scattered over an island ringed by three rivers; bell-shaped chedi towers and Khmer-style prangs dominate
classic 'reclining head in banyan roots' photo is at Wat Mahathat; the city was sacked by the Burmese in 1767
entries.found: 75 km north of Bangkok; a UNESCO-listed city of temple ruins, easily reached by train
entries.notes: Brick headsless Buddhas in a flat green plain - the ruin aesthetic here is everywhere but subtle: crumbling brick, red soil and coconut palms.

entries.name: Bagan (plain of temples)
entries.purpose: Buddhist royal capital; ~3,000 temples and monasteries in one plain
layout: an 80 km2 arid plain by the Irrawaddy river sprinkled with hundreds of red-brick temples and white stupas
travel between temples by e-bike at sunrise; sheer quantity is the experience, not one monument
entries.found: in the dry zone of Myanmar, 190 km south of Mandalay; the Irrawaddy runs past the temple field
entries.notes: Buildings range from shrine-size to 60 m towers; you can climb many. Seismic damage is constant - earthquakes (2016) knocked tops off. Red haze at dawn is the classic view.

entries.name: Hadrian's Wall
entries.purpose: Roman frontier wall; divided Britannia from Caledonia
layout: a dead-straight 128 km barrier from Solway Firth to the River Tyne - 80 Roman miles
east half stone, west half turf on foundations; forts and milecastles at intervals, ditch north of the line
entries.found: across northern England; walking the whole wall takes about a week
entries.notes: One of the longest single linear ruins on Earth; most of it is now a low, grassy ridge with occasional excavated stretches (e.g. Vindolanda). footprint_m is [length, width] - it is not a building.

entries.name: Timgad (Thamugadi)
entries.era: founded 100 CE; abandoned c. 8th c CE
entries.purpose: Trajanic veteran colony; model of Roman military town-planning
layout: a perfect 355 m square grid around a cardo and decumanus, 20 m blocks, 110+ insulae
the Severan-era city grew beyond the walls; sand covered it until 1765 when Napoleon's troops found it
entries.found: in the Aurès foothills of Algeria, 110 km south of Constantine; nicknamed 'African Pompeii'
entries.notes: The single clearest grid-planned ruin you will ever walk - square blocks read like a blueprint from the air. Sandstone honeys up to ochre in evening light.

entries.name: Fatehpur Sikri
entries.purpose: abandoned Mughal imperial capital (Akbar); monumental palace-mosque city
layout: a rhombus-shaped walled city on a rocky ridge, gridded streets and monuments along one long axis
Buland Darwaza 54 m tall is the tallest gateway in Mughal India; the city was abandoned partly for lack of water
entries.found: 40 km west of Agra, India; ghost city of red sandstone against dry scrub
entries.notes: A planned city abandoned after only ~15-40 years; the whole thing stands roofed and empty. White marble and red sandstone contrast hard - superb for a 'sealed royal quarter' scene.

entries.name: Nan Madol
entries.purpose: Saudeleur dynasty ceremonial capital; artificial islets and royal canals
layout: a 1.5 km by 0.7 km lagoon-edge complex of prismatic basalt header-and-stretcher walls built on coral rubble islets
walls up to 7 m high; no mortar, no metal tools - all fitted stone columns 0.5-5 t each
entries.found: off Temwen Island, south-east Pohnpei, Federated States of Micronesia; entered by boat through mangrove canals
entries.notes: Nicknamed the Venice of the Pacific; mangrove is reclaiming the canals and the site is UNESCO World Heritage in Danger. Walls of black stone amid green water - deeply atmospheric.

entries.name: Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum
entries.purpose: subterranean necropolis; three levels of rock-cut chambers
layout: 34+ rooms on three descending levels, cut entirely underground into limestone; acoustics amplify a voice in the Oracle Room
decorated with red ochre spirals; bodies were interred in niches and pits for ~1,500 years
entries.found: a lane in Paola, Malta; entered through an ordinary modern townhouse
entries.notes: The world's only prehistoric underground temple; visitors are limited to ~80 per day to protect the carving. Quintessential 'hidden door under an ordinary building' hook.
